usage: Sino-Korean reading of 0; the default in math, scores, and temperature
after the decimal point each digit is read one by one
영(zero) + 下 하(below); the standard weather word for minus temperatures
대(對 'against') links the two sides of a score
examples: 오 더하기 영은 오예요.
Five plus zero is five.
Simplest case: 영 as a plain math value, read exactly like the digit 0.
오늘 아침은 영하 오 도였어요.
This morning it was minus five degrees.
영하 is the everyday way to say 'sub-zero'; note it is one word, not 영 + 하.
축구 경기가 영 대 영으로 끝났어요.
The soccer match ended zero to zero.
Reporting a real scoreline: 대 sits between the two numbers like English 'to'.
nuance: 영 is the Sino-Korean reading of the digit 0 (한자 零, 'nothing/nil'), and it is the form you reach for in mathematics, temperatures, scores, percentages, and the figures after a decimal point. Its near-rival is 공 (孔/空-style reading): both translate as 'zero', but the dividing line is sharp — 영 is for quantities and measured values (영 도 = 0 degrees, 영 점 = 0 points), whereas 공 is for zeros recited inside a string of digits like phone and room numbers (공일공). They are NOT freely swappable. It collocates tightly with 영하 (below zero), 영 점 (0.0…), and 영 대 영 (a 0-0 tie). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, do not reuse 영 when reading out '010' or '302' — a Korean would never say 영일영; second, there is no native-Korean counting word for zero at all, so when you need 'zero' you are always choosing between these two Sino readings, never a 하나-series word.

mistakes: Reading the 0 in a phone number as 영 (영일영) — strings of recited digits take 공, so 010 is 공일공.
Hunting for a 'native' zero to match 하나/둘/셋 — there is none; both 영 and 공 are Sino, and you pick by context (measured value vs. recited digit).
Saying 영하 as two stressed words or inserting a particle (영 가 하) — it is a single fixed noun 영하 meaning 'below zero'.

usage: the 0 spoken aloud inside phone, room, and account numbers
the universal Korean mobile prefix, read digit by digit
공 voices the middle 0; 호 is the room/unit counter
examples: 제 번호 앞자리는 공일공이에요.
The front part of my number is 010.
Simplest use: reading the standard mobile prefix one digit at a time.
방 번호가 오공오 호예요.
The room number is 505.
Hotels and dorms recite room numbers digit by digit, so the middle 0 is 공.
서울은 지역 번호가 공이번이에요.
Seoul's area code is 02.
Real situation: distinguishing the 02 (공이) prefix when someone asks where to dial.
nuance: 공 is how Koreans voice the digit 0 when reading off a sequence of digits — phone numbers, area codes, room numbers, building codes, account and card numbers. Although the dictionary gloss is identical to 영 ('zero'), the two split cleanly by function: 공 is for digits you recite one-by-one in an identifier, while 영 is for a measured quantity (temperature, score, decimal). The dividing test: if the whole 'number' is really a label or address rather than an amount, use 공. It habitually appears in fixed strings — 공일공 (010), 공이 (02), and any 호(號) room number with a 0 inside. The English-speaker pitfall is importing the English habit of saying 'zero' or 'oh' interchangeably and then defaulting to 영: a phone number read as 영일영 sounds plainly wrong to natives. Also note 공 is invariable here — you do not pluralize or add a counter; you simply chain the digits (공-일-공) in a flat, even rhythm.

usage: 二十: 이(2) × 십(10), the Sino-Korean tens-builder
ratios and discounts use Sino numbers
examples: 일에서 이십까지 세어 보세요.
Count from one to twenty.
Plainest use: 이십 as the end-point of a Sino-Korean count.
지금 두 시 이십 분이에요.
It's 2:20 now.
Clock split: the hour is native (두 시) but the minutes are Sino (이십 분).
오늘은 유월 이십 일이라서 월급날이에요.
Today is June 20th, so it's payday.
Real situation: a calendar date, where 이십 일 reads '20th' with Sino numbers.
nuance: 이십 is the Sino-Korean twenty, transparently built as 二十 — 이(two) stacked on 십(ten) — and this stacking logic extends all the way up the tens. Its native counterpart is 스물/스무, and the contrast is the single biggest hurdle for beginners: Sino 이십 governs minutes, calendar dates, money, percentages, math, and any number over about a hundred, while native 스물 governs hours on a clock, ages, and most counted objects (스무 명, 스무 살). The collocations to lock in are 이십 분 (twenty past), 이십 일 (the 20th), and 이십 퍼센트. The classic English-speaker pitfall is treating '20' as one word and using 이십 everywhere — but '20 o'clock' is native (스무 시 is rare; people say 여덟 시 in the evening), and '20 years old' is 스무 살, never 이십 살. A useful rule of thumb: measured/abstract quantities lean Sino, hand-counted things and the hour lean native.

mistakes: Saying 이십 시 / 이 시 for the hour — clock hours are native, so 2 o'clock is 두 시, not 이십/이 시.
Saying 이십 살 for age — age uses native, so '20 years old' is 스무 살.
Forgetting the word order of compounds — 20 is 이십 (二十), but 12 is 십이 (十二); the multiplier-then-ten order is fixed.

usage: the most frequent use — telling time
일(日) as a date or a day-count
초(秒) seconds also take Sino numbers
examples: 삼십에서 십을 빼면 이십이에요.
Thirty minus ten is twenty.
Simplest use: 삼십 as a pure arithmetic value.
지금 일곱 시 삼십 분이에요.
It's 7:30 now.
Half past: native hour 일곱 시 plus Sino 삼십 분 — the everyday way to say 7:30.
환불은 삼십 일 안에 해야 해요.
Refunds must be made within thirty days.
Real situation: a policy window, where 삼십 일 means '30 days' as a duration.
nuance: 삼십 is the Sino-Korean thirty (三十, 삼 over 십), and for learners it earns its keep mainly in telling time, because '...:30' / half past comes up in nearly every spoken time. The native rival 서른 covers age (서른 살) and bare object counts, while 삼십 owns minutes, seconds, dates, durations, and money. Watch the meaning of 일(日) after it: 삼십 일 is either 'the 30th' (a date) or 'thirty days' (a span), disambiguated only by context — 삼십 일에 (on the 30th) vs. 삼십 일 동안 (for thirty days). Habitual collocations: 삼십 분 (half past), 삼십 일 (the 30th / 30 days), 삼십 초. The English-speaker pitfall is leaving off 분: '7:30' must be 일곱 시 삼십 분, and saying only 일곱 시 삼십 sounds unfinished; equally, never promote 삼십 into the hour slot (삼십 시 does not exist as a clock hour in ordinary speech).

usage: stack the ones digit straight on: 사십+오
examples: 사십은 십이 네 개예요.
Forty is four tens.
Simplest use: 사십 unpacked as 4×10, reinforcing the build.
여기서 학교까지 사십 분쯤 걸려요.
It takes about forty minutes from here to school.
Everyday duration; 쯤 ('about') softens the estimate.
이 가방은 사십만 원이에요.
This bag costs 400,000 won.
Real situation: quoting a price, where 사십만 reads with the 만 grouping.
nuance: 사십 is the Sino-Korean forty (四十), and like every Sino ten it is fully compositional: glue the ones digit on with no spacer, so 45 is 사십오 and 48 is 사십팔. It rules minutes, prices, percentages, and distances, while the native 마흔 is reserved for age (마흔 살) and a few hand-counts. A pronunciation note worth flagging: 사(四) is a single short syllable, and because Korean has several look-alike one-syllable numbers (사 4, 삼 3, 오 5), beginners must keep it crisp or '사십' blurs into a neighbour. Typical collocations: 사십 분, 사십만 원, 사십 퍼센트. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping money one-to-one onto Western grouping: 400,000 is not 'four hundred thousand' built on 천, but 사십만 — forty units of 만(10,000) — so you must regroup by four digits, not three. And as always, 사십 never names an age (use 마흔) or a clock hour.

Clipping 사 so it merges with 삼/오 — keep the digit distinct, since 사십(40), 삼십(30), 오십(50) differ by one syllable.

usage: the headline number on sale signs
examples: 반은 백의 오십 퍼센트예요.
Half is fifty percent of a hundred.
Simplest use: 오십 in a clean ratio statement.
지금 아홉 시 오십 분이라 곧 열 시예요.
It's 9:50, so it'll be ten soon.
Everyday clock-reading; native hour 아홉 시 with Sino 오십 분.
이 신발 오십 퍼센트 할인이라 바로 샀어요.
These shoes were fifty percent off, so I bought them right away.
Real situation: a sale, where 오십 퍼센트 할인 is the fixed 'half-price' phrase.
nuance: 오십 is the Sino-Korean fifty (五十), and beyond time it is the number you meet most on shop signs, because 오십 퍼센트 할인 ('50% off') is the great rallying cry of Korean sales. It governs minutes, money, scores, and percentages; the native rival 쉰 carries age (쉰 살). Composition is regular — 오십삼 (53), 오십칠 (57) — with the ones digit fused directly on. Core collocations: 오십 분, 오십 퍼센트, 오십 원. A small sound caution: 오(五) alone is 'five', so listen for the 십 that turns it into 'fifty'; in fast speech beginners sometimes hear 오 and miss the tens. The English-speaker pitfall is, again, the slots reserved for native numbers — '50 years old' is 쉰 살, not 오십 살, and there is no 오십 시 hour on a clock. When in doubt: a measured amount or ratio is Sino (오십), a person's age is native (쉰).

usage: 세(歲) pairs with Sino numbers in formal age
examples: 일 분은 육십 초예요.
One minute is sixty seconds.
Simplest use: a basic time fact, all Sino numbers.
여기까지 오는 데 육십 분 넘게 걸렸어요.
It took over sixty minutes to get here.
Everyday duration; 넘게 ('more than') leans on the count 육십.
저희 할아버지는 올해 육십 세가 되셨어요.
My grandfather turned sixty this year.
Real situation: formal age with the honorific 되셨어요, so 세 (not 살) takes Sino 육십.
nuance: 육십 is the Sino-Korean sixty (六十). Beyond seconds and minutes, it introduces a register split English speakers often miss: age can be said two ways, and the counter decides the number system. The formal/written counter 세(歲) takes Sino numbers — 육십 세 — and shows up on documents, news, and respectful speech, while the everyday counter 살 takes the native number 예순 (예순 살). So 'sixty years old' is 육십 세 OR 예순 살, but crossing them (육십 살 / 예순 세) is wrong. Pronunciation note: 육(六) is initial-ㅇ here but links smoothly into 십, and many speakers nasalize the boundary (yuk-ssip). Habitual collocations: 육십 초, 육십 분, 육십 세. The pitfall, then, is the counter-number agreement: pick 세 with Sino (육십 세) for formality, or 살 with native (예순 살) for daily talk — never mix the two halves.

Pairing 세 with a native number (예순 세) — the formal counter 세 takes Sino, giving 육십 세.
Reversing the digits as 십육 (16) when you mean 육십 (60) — multiplier-before-십 fixes the order.

examples: 칠십은 칠 곱하기 십이에요.
Seventy is seven times ten.
Simplest use: 칠십 unpacked as 7×10.
이번 시험에서 칠십 점밖에 못 받았어요.
I only got seventy points on this test.
Everyday result; 밖에 + negative verb means 'only', framing 칠십 점 as low.
할머니께서 올해 칠십 세 생신을 맞으셨어요.
Grandmother reached her seventieth birthday this year.
Real situation: a milestone birthday in honorific speech, so 세 takes Sino 칠십.
nuance: 칠십 is the Sino-Korean seventy (七十). It is the number of test scores (칠십 점), distances (칠십 미터), prices, and formal ages (칠십 세), and it composes regularly: 칠십이 (72), 칠십오 (75). As with 60, the age register splits by counter — formal 칠십 세 (Sino) versus everyday 일흔 살 (native 일흔). The collocation worth memorizing is 점(點) for scores, which always rides Sino numbers, so a grade is 칠십 점, never a native count. Pronunciation: 칠(七) ends in ㄹ and flows into 십, kept as two crisp syllables. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: first, scores feel 'countable' to English minds, tempting a native number, but 점 demands Sino (칠십 점); second, the age mismatch again — say 일흔 살 in conversation and reserve 칠십 세 for respectful or formal contexts, but never blend them into 칠십 살 or 일흔 세.

Flipping to 십칠 (17) for 칠십 (70) — the tens-multiplier (칠) comes before 십.

examples: 팔십은 팔에 십을 곱한 거예요.
Eighty is eight multiplied by ten.
Simplest use: spelling out the 8×10 build of 팔십.
지금 휴대폰 배터리가 팔십 퍼센트 남았어요.
My phone battery is at eighty percent now.
Everyday tech talk; 남았어요 ('is left') pairs naturally with a percentage.
설문에서 팔십 퍼센트가 찬성했어요.
Eighty percent agreed in the survey.
Real situation: reporting a statistic, where 팔십 퍼센트 is a proportion of respondents.
nuance: 팔십 is the Sino-Korean eighty (八十), the everyday number of battery levels, survey results, scores, and percentages, and it composes by simple stacking: 팔십육 (86), 팔십삼 (83). Its native counterpart 여든 again handles casual age (여든 살), versus formal 팔십 세. The collocation pattern to internalize is 퍼센트 — percentages are ratios, so they always take Sino numbers, making 팔십 퍼센트 the natural phrasing for '80% battery' or '80% agreed'. usage: 九十: 구(9) × 십(10), the last ten before 백(100)
the top of the two-digit Sino range
examples: 구십 다음은 백이에요.
After ninety comes a hundred.
Simplest use: locating 구십 just below the 백(100) rollover.
휴대폰이 구십 퍼센트까지 충전됐어요.
My phone charged up to ninety percent.

이번 시험은 구십 점이 넘어야 통과예요.
On this exam you must score over ninety to pass.
Real situation: a pass threshold, where 구십 점 is the cutoff.

usage: a common monthly-salary and big-ticket price figure
이 + 백만, the ones-multiplier sits in front
examples: 만이 백 개면 백만이에요.
A hundred ten-thousands make a million.
Simplest use: showing the 만-based build (100 × 10,000).
이 노트북이 백만 원이 조금 넘어요.
This laptop is a little over a million won.
Everyday price; 넘다 ('exceed') pairs with the figure 백만 원.
콘서트 표가 일 분 만에 백만 장이 팔렸어요.
A million tickets sold in one minute.
Real situation: a headline-style sales figure with the counter 장 (sheets/tickets).
nuance: 백만 is one million (百萬), literally 백(hundred) multiplied by 만(ten-thousand), and it exposes the deepest structural difference between Korean and English numbers: Korean groups by four digits (만 = 10,000), not three (thousand). So a million is not a free-standing 'million' word but a composite of 백 × 만, and 2,000,000 simply prefixes the multiplier as 이백만. There is no native rival here — large numbers are exclusively Sino. The everyday collocations are 백만 원 (a million won, the scale of salaries and laptops) and 백만 명/장 (a million people/tickets). The English-speaker pitfall is enormous and worth drilling: you cannot translate 'one million' digit-group by digit-group through 천(thousand). If you mentally chunk 1,000,000 as '1,000 × 1,000' you will reach for 천, but Korean parses it as '100 × 10,000' → 백만. Train yourself to insert a comma every four digits (100,0000) rather than every three, and the 만/억 units fall into place naturally.

usage: 億: the unit one step above 만, i.e. 만 × 만
일 + 억; the multiplier 일 is usually kept
the standard unit for apartment and house prices
examples: 만의 만 배가 일억이에요.
Ten thousand times ten thousand is one hundred million.
Simplest use: deriving 억 as 만 × 만 (10,000²).
서울 아파트는 보통 몇억씩 해요.
Seoul apartments usually cost several hundred million each.
Everyday housing talk; 몇억 ('several 억') and 씩 ('apiece') are very natural here.
그 사람이 복권으로 십억 원에 당첨됐대요.

Real situation: a windfall, where 십억 (10 × 억 = 1,000,000,000) is reported second-hand with -대요.

In Korea this is not an exotic 'big number' — it is the everyday currency of real estate, since apartments and houses are quoted in 억 (보통 몇억). The usual collocation keeps a multiplier in front: 일억, 삼억, 십억, plus the money counter 원. The English-speaker pitfall is the false friend with English magnitude words: 억 is NOT 'a million' and not even cleanly 'a hundred million' in the way English chunks it — because Korean groups by four digits, 1억 = 1,0000,0000. If you try to anchor 억 to a three-digit-grouped English word you will be off by an order of magnitude. The reliable move is positional: 만 is the 5th digit, 억 is the 9th digit. Note too that 일억 normally keeps its 일 (unlike 백 or 천, which can stand alone), so 'one hundred million won' is 일억 원.

usage: 番: counter for an assigned position or ID, with Sino numbers
list items, exam questions, jersey or seat numbers
asking for a bus, room, exit, or question number
examples: 이거 몇 번이에요?
What number is this?
Simplest use: 몇 번 asking the assigned number of an item.
저는 지하철 삼 번 출구에서 기다릴게요.
I'll wait at subway exit number 3.
Everyday meet-up; 삼 번 출구 names a specific exit with Sino 삼.
오 번 버스를 타고 두 번 갈아탔어요.
I took bus number 5 and transferred twice.
Real situation: one sentence shows both 번s — ID 오 번 (Sino) and 'twice' 두 번 (native).
nuance: 번 (한자 番) is the counter for an assigned, ordered number — bus and route numbers, subway exits, exam questions, list items, jersey and seat numbers — and in this ID sense it always takes Sino-Korean numbers: 삼 번 출구, 오 번 버스, never 세 번 출구. Its tricky twin is the homograph 번 meaning 'times/occasions', which takes NATIVE numbers: 세 번 (three times), 다섯 번 (five times). The dividing line is meaning, not spelling: does 번 label a thing (use Sino) or count repetitions (use native)? A near-synonym for the labelling sense is 호(號), but 호 attaches to rooms and issue/model numbers (302호, 창간호) while 번 covers routes, exits, and questions. The English-speaker pitfall is the Sino/native split inside a single counter: learners who have just mastered '세 번 = three times' over-apply native numbers to bus and exit numbers, producing 세 번 버스 — which a Korean parses as 'the bus, three times', not 'bus number 3'. Anchor it with the contrast pair 삼 번 (No. 3) vs. 세 번 (3 times).

usage: 層: counter for building levels, with Sino numbers
the go-to question in an elevator or a store
examples: 저는 삼 층에 살아요.
I live on the third floor.
Simplest use: stating a floor with the location particle 에.
몇 층에 가세요? 누를게요.
What floor are you going to? I'll press it.
Everyday elevator exchange; 몇 층 asks the floor before pressing the button.
화장품 매장은 지하 일 층에 있어요.
The cosmetics section is on basement level 1.
Real situation: department-store directions, where 지하 일 층 marks B1.
nuance: 층 (한자 層, 'layer/story') is the counter for floors of a building, and like other Sino-derived counters it always takes Sino numbers — 일 층, 이 층, 삼 층 — so it patterns with 번/호 and never with native 한/두/세. It is one of the highest-frequency counters in daily life: elevators, malls, apartments, and offices all run on it, and the survival question 몇 층에 가세요? ('what floor?') greets you in nearly every elevator. The basement uses 지하(地下) plus a Sino number counting downward, so B1 is 지하 일 층 and B2 is 지하 이 층. A useful contrast: 층 counts the floor you are on, whereas to count how many floors a building HAS as objects you can still say ...층짜리 (오 층짜리 건물, 'a five-story building'). The English-speaker pitfall is importing native numbers from object-counting habits (세 층 for the 3rd floor) — but 층 is firmly Sino, so it is 삼 층; and remember Korean '일 층' is the ground floor (like the US 1st floor), not the floor above the ground.
